welcome.intro: Wikitail is a small tool for writing articles and grounding them in sources you pick — pages from Wikipedia, images from Wikimedia Commons, records from Finna. Each article keeps a tail: a curated list of the material it draws on, with your own notes on why each piece is there. When an article is published it becomes part of the site anyone signed in can read.
welcome.empty: You are not part of any project yet. A project manager can add you — ask whoever runs your site to get in touch.

tutorial.title: Quick guide for editors
tutorial.intro: This guide shows how to write an article, bring in material from external sources and publish it. The example article is called Sauna. Button names in the editor are shown as they appear on screen.

home.title: Sign in and open a project
home.body1: After signing in you see the home page. It has a Your name field. The name appears at the top of PDF exports. If the field is empty, the part of your email before the {'@'} sign is used. You can change the name at any time and press Save.
home.body2: Below that is the list of projects you belong to. Click a project to open it.
home.note: If you see no projects, ask a project manager to add you as a member.

project.title: Create an article
project.body1: The project page lists the project's articles. To create one, type a title, pick a language and a licence (default CC BY 4.0) and press Create article. A new article is always a draft that only project members can see.
project.note: Who can edit: only the user who created an article (its owner) or an administrator can edit it. You can read other people's articles, but not edit them, even in the same project.

editor.title: Write the article
editor.body1: Open an article by clicking its title. The editor is split into tabs:
editor.item1: Article: the article text. You write Markdown on the left and see a preview on the right. Markdown help explains the formatting.
editor.item2: Article library and Tail: the material that belongs to the article (see below).
editor.item3: Wiki world, Commons, Finna, Local: the sources you import material from.
editor.after1: Press Save draft to save. Changes are not saved until you press the button.
editor.after2: Next to the language you see the article's language versions. Click for example + EN to create a translation. A translation is its own article, and you are its owner.

import.title: Import material from sources
import.body1: All material is first collected in the article library. From there you can embed it in the text or add it to the tail. Open one of the source tabs:
import.item1: Wiki world: pages from Wikipedia and Wikidata.
import.item2: Commons: freely licensed images, audio and video.
import.item3: Finna: material from Finnish archives, libraries and museums.
import.item4: Local: your own files. You choose the licence and the credit.
import.after1: Type a search term, press Search and then Import next to the result you want. The item is saved in the library with its author and licence.
import.after2: Imported items appear on the Article library tab.

embed.title: Embed material in the text
embed.body1: A library item can be placed in the article text with a shortcode such as {code}.
embed.item1: On the Article tab, press Show library.
embed.item2: Place the cursor in the text where you want the item.
embed.item3: Press Insert next to the library item. The shortcode is added at the cursor and the preview shows the item right away.

tail.title: Build the tail
tail.body1: The tail is a curated list of sources shown after the article. Each item has your own comment about why it is included.
tail.item2: Under Add from your library, press Add next to an item.
tail.item3: Write a comment for the item. It is saved when you leave the field.
tail.item4: Reorder items by dragging the handle (⠿) and remove an item with the × button.

publish.title: Publish
publish.body1: When the article is ready, press Publish. The status changes to published and the article becomes visible to everyone. You can keep editing after publishing. To hide the article again, save it with Save draft.
publish.body2: The published article shows the text, source credits and, at the end, the tail with your comments.

pdf.title: Download a PDF
pdf.body1: The page of a published article has a Download PDF link at the top. The PDF contains the article, images, sources and the tail. The name you set on the home page appears at the top.
pdf.body2: PDF export requires signing in, and only published articles can be downloaded.

delete.title: Delete an article
delete.body1: Use the red Delete button at the bottom of the editor. Only the article's owner and administrators can delete an article.
delete.item1: If the article has other language versions, only this language version and its tail are deleted. The other versions and the shared library are kept.
delete.item2: If you delete the last language version, its library is deleted too.

help.title: How Wikitail works
help.projectsBody1: A project is a small collection of articles about a shared subject — a course, a research theme, an exhibition. Every article belongs to one project, and every project has one or more languages it publishes in.
help.projectsBody2: An article is a piece of writing you author here. Alongside its text it carries a tail: a hand-picked list of pages, images, or records from outside sources that supported the writing, each with a short note from you on why it is there. Readers see the article, then the tail; the tail is the citation and the recommendation at once.
help.draftBody: A new article starts as a draft — only members of its project can see it while it takes shape. Setting the status to published makes it visible to anyone signed in to Wikitail. Publishing does not lock the article; you can keep editing, and the newest version is what readers see.
help.libraryBody1: The article library is where you gather source material. You can search Wikipedia and Wikidata for background, Wikimedia Commons for freely licensed media, and Finna for material from Finnish archives and museums. You can also upload your own files with a licence you pick. Each imported item is stored with its credit and licence, and can be added to a tail with a single click.
help.libraryBody2: Wikipedia articles are handled two ways at project level: live links keep only enough to point at the current page, and hard copies also keep the text as it read when it was imported. Media is always copied either way, so readers do not hotlink to Commons.
help.languagesBody: A project declares which languages it uses. When you translate an article, the two language versions stay linked: readers switching language stay on the same subject, and importing a Commons image in one language quietly pulls in its Wikipedia caption in every other project language.
help.rolesReader: Reader — anyone signed in. Can read published articles.
help.rolesEditor: Editor of a project — can write and edit articles, curate tails, and upload files in that project. Cannot change project settings.
help.rolesManager: Manager of a project — everything an editor can do, plus change languages, publishing mode, and add or remove members.
help.rolesAdmin: Admin of the site — can do everything on every project, and add new projects and users from the admin tools page.
help.start1: Open a project from the welcome page.
help.start2: Create a new article, or open an existing one to edit it.
help.start3: In the editor, use the source tabs on the right to import background material and media into the article library.
help.start4: Drop a library item into the article body with a shortcode, or add it to the tail with your own comment on why it belongs there.
help.start5: When it is ready, change the status to published.
